title: Ardas in grief
hook: the Ardas for the dead asks peace for the one who has gone, and for those left, the strength to accept the Will

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ardas before a journey, and your line: ask before you go. What did you name before you started? Today, the hardest door the Ardas walks through. Go gently. Day six hundred forty-one.

A family stands in a gurdwara a few days after a funeral. Some of them haven't slept. Someone is holding a framed photo; someone else is holding a toddler who doesn't understand why everyone is so quiet. In the days since the death, the Guru Granth Sahib has been read, perhaps from beginning to end. Now the reading is finished. The congregation rises, and the Ardas begins. And somewhere in it, the name of the one who died is spoken aloud, for the last time in this way.
screen: `A FAMILY, A FEW DAYS AFTER.` → `THE READING IS FINISHED.` → `THE NAME IS SPOKEN ALOUD.`

segments.voice: Sikhs usually cremate their dead. At the cremation, and again each night at home, Kirtan Sohila, the evening hymns, is sung. Over the following days, many families hold a reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, and when it ends, an Ardas is said that many call the antim ardas, the final prayer. The petition in that Ardas asks two things. First, for the one who has gone: that their soul find rest, a place at the Guru's feet, union with the One. Second, for the ones left: the strength to accept the Will. That word, will, is bhaana. It runs all through Sikh teaching. Bhaana mannan, accepting the Will, is one of the hardest and most honored things a Sikh can do. Guru Arjan put it in a line many grieving families hold onto. In Raag Asa, on ang 394, he says, in effect: what You do seems sweet to me; Nanak asks only for the treasure of the Name. Now, an honest note. Accepting the Will doesn't mean pretending it doesn't hurt. Sikh teaching discourages loud wailing and ritual mourning displays, and it treats death as part of the One's order rather than a punishment. But it doesn't forbid tears. Accepting the Will is something people grow into, sometimes over years, and the Ardas doesn't demand that it be finished by Sunday. It asks for the strength to keep moving toward it. And notice: the family isn't asked to do this alone. The whole congregation stands with them, and the line rising spirits, good for all, is said even here.
screen: `KIRTAN SOHILA AT THE CREMATION.` · `REST FOR THE ONE WHO HAS GONE.` · `BHAANA: THE WILL.` · `ACCEPTANCE TAKES TIME.` · then, large: `IN HIS WILL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and take it at whatever depth feels right today. Bring to mind someone you miss: a grandparent, a friend, even a pet, or someone who isn't gone but is far away. Let their face come. If it hurts, let it hurt a little. Breathe. Then, if you pray, you can ask peace for them, and the strength to accept what you can't change, in your own words or with a quiet Waheguru. If not, simply wish them peace. Stay with them until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Ardas in grief. After a death, the Ardas asks rest for the one who has gone, and for the family, the strength to accept the Will, bhaana.
Your line: in his will. Today, if you know someone who is grieving, send them one line, just that you're thinking of them. Nothing to fix. Day six hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: After a death, Sikhs sing Kirtan Sohila at the cremation, often hold a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and close it with an Ardas asking rest for the departed and acceptance of the Will for the family.
